articles.title: Post your questions for Michael Winterbottom
articles.summary: With us to mark the 24th anniversary of 24 Hour Party People, the director’s work includes everything from Cracker to A Cock and Bull Story, Wonderland to Welcome to Sarajevo. And, of course, The Trip.
body: Of course, the 90s couldn’t be any more in vogue at the minute – but the 90s couldn’t have happened without the 80s. And that’s where 24 Hour Party People comes in, Michael Winterbottom’s riotous 2002 film that charts Manchester’s music scene from the Sex Pistols’ legendary 1976 Lesser Free Trade Hall gig through Factory Records, Joy Division, New Order and into the Madchester era of Happy Mondays and the Haçienda. It’s the story of Manchester music before Oasis swaggered in and took over the world, and it stars Paddy Considine, Shirley Henderson, Andy Serkis and John Simm – plus Steve Coogan as the late broadcaster and Factory Records boss Tony Wilson.

He has also regularly reunited with Coogan, most famously for 2010’s The Trip and its sequels, in which Coogan and Brydon travelled, ate and attempted increasingly competitive celebrity impressions – including a Michael Caine-off that became almost as famous as the films themselves. The trio are now making a fifth instalment, The Trip to the Northern Lights, which sees Coogan and Brydon eating, bickering and impersonating their way through Scandinavia and the Nordic countries.

articles.summary: Jane Austen is getting a style upgrade just in time for the latest trip to the Dashwood family estate. Designer Sarah Flint has teamed with Focus Features on a new capsule collection inspired by the upcoming “Sense and Sensibility” adaptation, translating the contrasting personalities of sisters…
body: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

The capsule also includes two hand-painted scarves: an Anemones Scarf painted by Flint herself and the Dashwood Scarf, created by longtime collaborator Katarzyna Strozynska-Goraj. Colors and motifs throughout the collection were pulled from the visual world of the film.

“Anemones are one of the classic English garden flowers, and in the old language of flowers, they mean anticipation,” Flint said. “We hand-embroidered it onto linen, the same slow, careful way women of that era would have worked, one stitch at a time, because printing it would have missed the point.”

For Flint, the collaboration was also something of an Austen fan project. “I’ve wanted to do something with this book for years, so when this collaboration came together, it felt like the equivalent of a superfan getting asked to plan a reunion tour,” she said. “I didn’t want a shoe with a movie logo slapped on it. I spent real time on where Elinor ends and Marianne begins, down to which thread color went on which shoe.”

articles.summary: Last week, politicians decided they could not let Hollywood slip away. First, California Gov. Gavin Newsom pushed for a resolution of the Paramount antitrust case out of fear that the studio would leave the state. And in Congress, Republicans and Democrats joined to introduce a U.S.
body: In both cases, the result is a deepening integration with the state. The Paramount antitrust settlement entails five years of government monitoring and commitments to keep ownership of studio lots, to produce a certain number of films and to install an oversight board as a watchdog for news networks CBS and CNN.

Neither side in the merger battle wanted this outcome. Paramount CEO David Ellison wanted to buy Warner Bros. Discovery without conditions but was willing to accept some state intrusion as the price of scale. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, meanwhile, wanted to block the deal outright or at minimum force divestitures.

“Structural remedies are always preferable to behavioral,” said Paula Blizzard, Bonta’s antitrust chief, at a seminar on Sept. 14, “because the government gets in, it says, ‘Change the structure; get more competitors,’ and then the government gets out.” A behavioral solution, she added, would require the state to become a “de facto participant” in the market.

articles.title: Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut
articles.summary: Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights.
body: ‘I decide my past,” says a village matriarch in this intriguingly political and poetic drama from Suzannah Mirghani, making her feature debut – and with it becoming the first Sudanese woman to direct a feature. (She was forced to cancel the original shoot in Sudan when war broke out in 2023, moving production to Egypt.) It’s a film with things to say about the long shadow of the British empire, neocolonialism, women’s rights and female genital mutilation. But it mostly says it all without undermining its sense of mystery and shivers of magic realism.

We’re in present day Sudan, where village elder Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud) is an iron-willed woman not to be messed with. Everyone knows the story of how as a young girl she ran the British out of town; small children in the village gleefully tell the story of how she slaughtered every single last one of them. Can it possibly be true? The trauma of her past is at the centre of the film, and Mahmoud’s witchy performance, fierce and powerful, is utterly compelling.

articles.title: Funko Unveils Ultra-Limited Marvel NYCC Figures, Including $100 Light-Up Sorcerer Supreme Doom
articles.summary: Funko is bringing some heavy Marvel firepower to New York Comic Con this year, including an ultra-limited light-up Doctor Doom figure that will be one of just 500 produced. The collectibles company has unveiled a new batch of Marvel Pop!
body: The $100 Doom is an in-person exclusive that will be sold in limited quantities at Funko’s NYCC booth. For collectors who don’t manage to snag the grail version, Funko is also releasing a standard Sorcerer Supreme Doom Pop! for $15, which will be available both at the convention and on Funko.com.

Also joining the lineup is a particularly bloodthirsty take on Spider-Man: a Vampire Miles Morales figure. Priced at $40, the 4.1-inch Pop! turns the fan-favorite wall-crawler into a fanged Marvel variant. Funko is producing 1,000 of the limited-edition figures, which will also come housed in a UV-protective case and be available in limited quantities at the company’s booth.

Wolverine collectors, meanwhile, will have an even tougher hunt on their hands. Funko’s $50 Ultimate Wolverine Pop! is limited to just 500 pieces and features the X-Men hero unmasked and claws out. Like the other high-end limited editions, it comes pre-packaged inside a Premium Plastic Pop! Protector.

All of the convention exclusives will sport a 2026 Fall Convention sticker and feature Funko’s new authentication packaging, which uses micro-optic technology and individual item codes that can be verified through Octane5.

body: People often ask me which classic films they could use to introduce their teenagers or children to movies made before this century. I think two of the best “gateway” movies for classic cinema are “Rear Window” and Sidney Lumet’s masterful 1957 debut, a movie that has lost none of its power in the almost seven decades since its release. Criterion has given this masterpiece the 4K upgrade this month with a new digital restoration, accompanied by the excellent special features from the first physical release, including the original 1954 teleplay version on which Lumet’s adaptation was based.
